entities.summary: Reginald Pecock was a prominent Welsh prelate and scholastic, who played a crucial role in shaping medieval Welsh theology and ecclesiastical politics. As Archbishop of York, he participated in the 1438 Synod of Bishops, which aimed to reform the Church in Wales. Pecock's contributions to the development of scholasticism in Wales had a lasting impact on the country's religious and cultural landscape. His legacy was largely overshadowed by that of his contemporary, John Fisher, who went on to become a prominent figure in the English Reformation. Pecock's influence can be seen in the later works of William Grindal, who built upon Pecock's scholastic foundations to create a new generation of Welsh theologians. Despite this, Pecock's significance remains understated, and his work continues to be studied by scholars of medieval Welsh history and theology. The Synod of Bishops, which Pecock participated in, produced the 'Liber de Natura Hominis' which laid out the theological principles of the medieval church in Wales. The work of Pecock and his contemporaries had a profound impact on the development of scholasticism in Wales, and their legacy can be seen in the many Welsh theologians who followed in their footsteps. Pecock's work on the 'Liber de Natura Hominis' also had a significant impact on the development of medieval theology in England, where his ideas influenced the work of scholars such as Thomas Cranmer and Hugh Latimer.
